content.intro: In this lesson, you will explore introduction to xml parsing within XML Parsing and Programming APIs. You will connect its syllabus topics to an inspectable example, check the expected result, and note tool/version limits.
content.why_it_matters: Introduction to XML Parsing matters because XML workflows rely on explicit structure and predictable processing. The lesson helps you reason about why parsing is necessary, avoid a common misunderstanding, and make a result reproducible for another developer.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A parser reads XML syntax and exposes a logical representation to application code. Tree APIs are convenient for navigation and editing; event or pull APIs can reduce memory for large inputs, at the cost of more state management.

content_blocks.title: Connect the subtopics
content_blocks.text: This lesson explicitly covers: Why parsing is necessary; XML text and parsed document structures; Parser responsibilities; Well-formedness checks during parsing. Treat these as connected parts of one workflow: define the structure, make the relevant assumptions explicit, and verify a result with a small known input.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Inspect this example as text. Run it only in a processor that supports the shown language/version; the standard CodeLeaf playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only and does not execute XML, XSD, XPath, XSLT, XQuery, Python, or SQL. Choose the API for the access pattern, not just familiarity: DOM for random tree navigation/editing, SAX for push events, StAX for pull-oriented event handling, and incremental parsing for bounded-memory processing.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the sample to its exact starting state before each experiment. Change one element, attribute, expression, or constraint at a time, then compare the result with the expected behavior.
content_blocks.limitations: This snippet is an inspectable example, not an XML execution service. Validate it with a standards-compatible XML processor; feature support depends on the processor/version.

content_blocks.title: Version and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Distinguish well-formedness, schema validity, and application-level correctness; they are different checks.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small synthetic example that demonstrates “Why parsing is necessary”. Then add one boundary case involving “XML text and parsed document structures”. Write down what should happen before testing, and record the exact output or processor message afterward.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a document is correct because it looks readable.
common_mistakes.why: Visual appearance does not prove well-formedness, schema validity, correct namespace handling, or application-level meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse and validate the document with the intended processor, then assert its meaning using a focused test.

common_mistakes.problem: Mixing specification features with processor support.
common_mistakes.why: A standard may define features that a specific runtime does not implement.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the version and feature support; test with the actual target processor.

common_mistakes.why: Missing values, wrong types, namespace differences, or boundary inputs can expose failures.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a valid case, an invalid case, and an edge case to the verification notes.
